meta.descriptionEn: On 24 October 1960, at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in the Kazakh steppe, the Soviet Union's prototype R-16 intercontinental missile stood fuelled on the pad, with a deadline to beat: the anniversary of the Revolution on 7 November. Then something went wrong in a way nobody had planned for. Why were so many senior officers and engineers standing near a fuelled rocket? What triggered the fault? And why did the state announce that its commander had died in a plane crash? This documentary follows the Nedelin catastrophe from the pressure that built it to the cover-up that hid it until 1989, the conflicting death tolls, the commission that investigated, and the lessons it left behind.

Itne bade afsar missile ke itne qareeb kyun the? Hadse ki wajah kya thi? Aur Marshal Nedelin ki maut ko plane crash kyun bataya gaya? Is documentary mein poori kahani Urdu aur English mein dekhein.

articleEn: On 24 October 1960, at the Baikonur Cosmodrome on the Kazakh steppe, a new missile stood on its launch pad while preparations for a test flight continued. It was a prototype R-16, an intercontinental ballistic missile, a weapon able to strike targets very far away. Its first test flight was about to take place.

Then, suddenly, the engine of the missile's second stage ignited on the pad itself. The first stage below burst apart, and fire and a massive blast spread across the site. Military and technical personnel were gathered around the missile at the time. It was loaded with fuel, and the people near it were caught in the flames.

Three questions hang over the story. Why were so many people so close to a fuelled rocket? Was it simply a mistake? And what was the real cause of the engine fault? The strangest part came afterward: the world was told that a plane had crashed. Soviet authorities kept news of the disaster hidden for decades, and said that Chief Marshal Mitrofan Nedelin had died in an air crash.

In this article we will go through the whole story: what happened at Pad 41, who was there, what the investigation found, and how the truth finally came out. This is more than the story of an explosion. It is the story of a secret that stayed hidden until 1989. So let's start from the beginning.

chapters.covers: Founded in 1955 on the Kazakh Steppe near Tyuratam as a test range for the R-7 ICBM. Site chosen by a commission under General Voznyuk, influenced by Korolyov. One of the costliest Soviet projects. Its primary purpose was ICBM testing. The U-2 photographed it in 1957. Sputnik and Gagarin launched from there. The Baikonur name and the misdirection theory.

articleEn: Our story begins at the Baikonur Cosmodrome, located today in Kazakhstan. By area, it is the largest operational space launch facility in the world. It was established in 1955 by a decree of the Soviet Ministry of Defense, and it served as the test center for the world's first ICBM, the R-7 Semyorka.

The site was chosen by a commission led by General Vasily Voznyuk, and Sergey Korolyov, Chief Designer of the R-7, also influenced the decision. The land had to be flat, because the rocket's radio control system needed continuous signals from ground stations hundreds of kilometres away. The missile's path also had to run away from populated areas, and a location nearer the equator is better for launches. The commission finally picked Tyuratam, a small village in the middle of the Kazakh steppe.

Launch facilities, hundreds of kilometres of new roads and railway lines all had to be built there, which made it one of the most expensive infrastructure projects in the Soviet Union. A town was also built for the workers, with housing, schools and other facilities. It became a city in 1966 and was named Leninsk.

Space was not Baikonur's only purpose. Until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, its main job was testing ballistic missiles. Its secret official name was State Test Range No. 5, and it stayed under Ministry of Defense control until the second half of the 1990s. On 5 August 1957, an American U-2 reconnaissance plane discovered the Tyuratam missile test range and photographed it. On 4 October 1957, Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, was launched from here, opening a new chapter in the Cold War space race. On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin made the first crewed orbital flight from the same place. The pad he left from is called Gagarin's Start.

Even the name Baikonur is a puzzle. According to most sources, it was deliberately chosen around 1961 to send the Western Bloc to the wrong place, a small mining town near Jezkazgan, about 320 kilometres to the northeast. But according to NASA's Apollo-Soyuz history, the name was not meant to mislead; it was simply what the area had been called before the cosmodrome was built. That was the secret spaceport. Next we meet the marshal whose name this disaster would carry.

articleEn: The man whose name is forever tied to this disaster is Mitrofan Ivanovich Nedelin. He was born on 9 November 1902 in Borisoglebsk, in the Voronezh Governorate of the Russian Empire. In 1920, at just 18, he joined the Red Army, and he served as a volunteer in the Russian Civil War until 1923. In 1924 he became a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and returned to the army as an artillery commander. From 1937 to 1939 he took part in the Spanish Civil War as a foreign volunteer on the side of the Republican Government.

After returning from Spain in 1940, he was made commander of the artillery of the 160th Rifle Division, and he also took part in the Winter War. When the Soviet Union entered World War II in 1941, Nedelin first led an Anti-Tank Brigade and then commanded the artillery of several armies. From 1943 to 1945 he was artillery commander of the 3rd Ukrainian Front, and he is said to have played a special role in the conquest of Hungary. For his wartime service he was named Hero of the Soviet Union on 28 April 1945, and he also received several Orders of Lenin and Red Banners.

His career kept rising after the war. In 1948 he became head of the chief artillery directorate, and from 1955 he was Deputy Minister of Defence. In 1959 he was made the first commander of the Strategic Rocket Forces, and on 8 May 1959 he reached the rank of Chief Marshal of the Artillery.

The question in the Cold War was how to deliver a nuclear warhead to America. Nedelin concluded that rockets were a better route than bombers. With that thinking, he ordered Sergei Korolev to build the massive R-7 ICBM, which could carry a large warhead to America. Interestingly, the R-7 never became an effective ICBM. But it was powerful enough to put Sputnik and Vostok into orbit. In this way Nedelin unknowingly played an important part in the start of the Space Age and kept the Soviet Union ahead in the early Space Race.
But in 1960, Nedelin headed the program for a new missile, the R-16. What was this missile like, and what dangers came with it?

articleEn: So what exactly was the R-16? It was the Soviet Union's first successful intercontinental ballistic missile to actually be deployed. In the West it was called the SS-7 Saddler, while inside Russia its GRAU index was 8K64. It was about 30 metres long, 3 metres in diameter, with a launch weight of 141 tons, a very large machine.

With a 5 to 6 Mt thermonuclear warhead it could reach 11,000 kilometres, and with a 3 Mt warhead its range extended to 13,000 kilometres. Its accuracy was limited, with a circular error probable of 2.7 kilometres. Soviet planners wanted a missile more practical than the R-7, which is often described as a zeroth-generation, largely experimental missile. The problem was that the R-7 used liquid oxygen as oxidiser, which made it hard to keep ready for launch over a long time.

The answer was a different kind of propellant. The R-16 used UDMH as fuel and RFNA as oxidiser. This was a hypergolic pair, meaning the two substances ignite on their own as soon as they meet. They were nicknamed the Devil's venom. They were chosen because their boiling temperature was high and they could be stored. That storability was their biggest advantage.

But there was a price. These substances were extremely corrosive and toxic. Because of the nitric acid, a fuelled missile could stay that way for only a few days. After that the fuel had to be removed and the missile sent back to the factory. A fuelled R-16 was therefore a dangerous and delicate thing. In normal duty the missiles stayed in hangars, and rolling them out, fuelling and preparing them took one to three hours.

The missile's control system was designed at OKB-692 in Kharkov, a city in the Ukrainian SSR. Another important name in this story is the missile designer Mikhail Yangel. The disaster later slowed his work but did not end it, and the R-16 eventually proved a success. By 1965 there were 202 missiles deployed, and it stayed in service until 1976. But we are still in 1960. Before the first flight, pressure was building that would prove very costly. Where did it come from?

articleEn: On 23 October 1960, the prototype R-16 was installed on launching pad 41 at Baikonur. It now awaited its final tests, as the missile was being readied for its first test flight. But one date hung over all the preparations: 7 November 1960, the anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution. Nedelin wanted the R-16 test launch to happen before then, and he insisted on it. The result was intense schedule pressure, at a time when the program was running into many major engineering difficulties.

Imagine a new, complex missile filled with corrosive and toxic fuel, and a deadline hanging over everyone's head. It was a dangerous mix. Safety requirements for such missiles already existed, and launch procedures accounted for these hazards. But when time is short, normal safety margins slowly weaken. Later analyses pointed to exactly this.

One big problem was that pre-launch tests and launch preparations began to overlap, so separate phases of work blended together. Normally work goes in order: first tests, then confidence, then launch preparation. Here that order had broken down. The missile's main sequencer had also been replaced. A sequencer is the system that runs different operations in the correct order, and this one would soon be at the centre of the story. We will come back to it.

The second danger was the number of people present. A later commission found far more people on the pad than necessary. Most of them should have been at a safe distance, in bunkers, but they were gathered around the fuelled missile. The bunkers were a few hundred metres from the pad, which was surrounded by a barbed-wire fence.

Why were so many people there? The sources give no simple answer. They only say that troubleshooting and launch preparations were going on at the same time, and people were near the missile. So there was a fuelled missile, a changed sequencer, and many people on the pad. Later safety analysis called it a broad failure of controls, procedures and management. The day of 24 October was approaching. Could the work be finished on time, and if not, what was about to happen?

chapters.covers: Fault in the sequencer fires the second-stage engine; first stage ruptures; explosion. Those near were incinerated, others burned or poisoned by toxic vapours. Sakharov's account of personnel running to the barbed-wire fence. The camera operator's automatic cameras. Nedelin and other leading figures lost. Yangel survived because he left to smoke behind a bunker, though he was burned.

articleEn: On 24 October 1960, on the Baikonur steppe, the fuelled R-16 stood on Pad 41 and pre-launch testing was under way. It helps to remember that this was not the moment of launch but a phase of testing before launch. Then suddenly something happened that should not have. Because of a fault in the replaced main sequencer, the second-stage engine ignited while the missile was still on the pad. The fire of the upper stage flared right above the lower stage. The structure of the first stage burst, and a huge explosion destroyed the entire missile.

What caused the fault? According to Chertok, after work on the sequencer, a wrong electrical sequence had formed in the control system. We will return to this at the end. Fire and blast spread around the pad at once. Military and technical personnel were gathered close to the missile. Those nearest to it did not survive even for moments. Others farther away were engulfed by fire and clouds of toxic fuel vapour.

Andrei Sakharov described many details of the scene. According to him, when the engine started, most of the people there ran toward the perimeter. But they were trapped inside the barbed-wire security fence, and the fireball of burning fuel swallowed them. Here is something important to understand: the fence around the pad was there for protection, but at that moment it became an obstacle for the people.

In the middle of this chaos, one person had a different task. A camera operator, before seeking shelter, remotely started the automatic cameras around the pad. These cameras recorded the blast in detail. So filmed evidence of the disaster existed, even though official silence followed.

The most prominent name among the dead was Chief Marshal Mitrofan Nedelin. One of his top aides also died with him. The USSR's top missile-guidance designer and more than 70 officers and engineers were killed in the blast as well. Some people died later. It is generally described as the deadliest launch accident connected to rockets or spaceflight, even though the R-16 was really being tested as a military missile.

One man escaped. Missile designer Mikhail Yangel was not there at the time. He had gone behind a bunker, a few hundred metres away, to smoke a cigarette. He was not entirely safe from the blast and suffered burns, but he lived, and that fact later became a question. In later years, the 1994 state commission report gave a total of 78 deaths, 74 killed at the scene and 4 who died later in hospital. Other estimates differ. As we will see in the next part, some sources say 54 and others 126 or even more. Smoke was rising over Pad 41. But the real question was what the world would be told.

articleEn: Right after the disaster of 24 October 1960, Nikita Khrushchev imposed complete secrecy on the event. An official news release said that Marshal Nedelin had died in a plane crash during an undisclosed mission. In truth, Nedelin, who headed the R-16 development program, had died on the pad while the prototype missile was being prepared. The families of other engineers were advised to say that their loved ones had also died in the same plane crash. Families had to repeat a false story alongside their grief, unable to openly tell the true story of their loved ones.

Khrushchev ordered Leonid Brezhnev to lead the investigating commission and go to the site. Brezhnev reached the firing range on 25 October 1960. There he said: 'Comrades! We do not want to take anyone to court. We will investigate the causes and take steps to continue the work.' Even so, I. A. Doroshenko was held responsible for the incident. Doesn't that seem contradictory? Brezhnev said the causes would be investigated.

The commission found that there were more people than necessary near the fuelled missile. It found far too many people on the launch pad, most of whom should have been in the safety of bunkers. This shows the reality of that day: the missile stood fuelled on the pad, troubleshooting was going on, and people were gathered near it. Later analyses also point to time pressure. The pressure to launch before the 7 November anniversary had weakened the usual safety margins.

Mikhail Yangel also comes into this part of the story. He had survived, and Khrushchev asked him a harsh question: 'Why did you stay alive?' The question sounds heavy enough, but the answer was even more startling. Yangel replied in a trembling voice, 'I went a little distance away to smoke a cigarette. This is all my fault.' Later Yangel suffered a heart attack and was away from work for several months. The weight of the disaster did not stay confined to the pad.

Meanwhile, all of this stayed hidden from the Soviet public. The story told about Nedelin's death held for decades. The secrecy was so complete that the Soviet Union itself did not publicly acknowledge the event until 1989. So when and how did the world learn the truth? And did people ever learn the real number? We look at that next.

articleEn: Now the biggest question: how many people died? Surprisingly, there is no single answer. Different sources give different numbers, and each answer tells the story of a different era, with rumour in one place, espionage in another and official records in another.

In December 1960, the Italian news agency Continentale gave the Western world its first report. According to it, 100 people, including Nedelin, had died. Continentale published this on 8 December 1960, citing unknown sources, so it was not based on any official announcement. Then in 1965, The Guardian cited information from the spy Oleg Penkovsky, and its report said up to 300 people had died. In 1976, exiled scientist and dissident Zhores Medvedev provided more details in the British magazine New Scientist, and the picture of what really happened slowly began to emerge.

There is also a declassified 1965 CIA report, discussed by Dwayne Day. It generally treated the information on the Soviet missile disaster as credible. But it rejected claims about nuclear propulsion. It linked the event to evidence of a failed ICBM launch attempt on 23 to 24 October 1960. There are also mentions of unusual activity connected with Tyuratam and Dnepropetrovsk after the disaster. Together these hints formed a bigger picture.

Finally, on 16 April 1989, the Soviet Union publicly acknowledged the event for the first time, in the weekly magazine Ogoniok. At that time it said only that a 'significant number' of people had died. Later the same year the government gave a figure of 54. One important official figure comes from the 1994 state commission report, which says 78 people died in total: 74 killed at the scene and 4 who died later in hospital. That is more than 54 but fewer than 126.

Then, on the 50th anniversary of the disaster, Roscosmos gave the figure of 126, which came from engineer Boris Chertok. But Roscosmos also said the true number could be anywhere between 60 and 150. Why do the sources differ so much? One possible reason is secrecy, since the real information did not come out for decades. Another source on Nedelin mentions about 120 other people. So estimates range from 54 to 300. These numbers show how hard it is to settle on an accurate count after secrecy. But a bigger question than the number is why the disaster happened. In the next part we look at the causes and the lessons.

chapters.covers: Chertok's account of an erroneous electrical sequence after work on the main sequencer, versus the wider failure of controls, procedures and management. The R-16 programme resumed in January 1961 and first flew on 2 February 1961, entering service in 1961. The memorial at Baikonur, Yeltsin's 1999 Order of Courage, and the R-9 fire of 24 October 1963 that made it Baikonur's 'Black Day'. Open questions about the true toll, and a request to like and subscribe.

articleEn: So what was the cause? According to Boris Chertok, the immediate cause of the premature ignition was a wrong electrical sequence in the control system, which arose after work on the main sequencer. At the technical level, the immediate cause was a fault. But later safety analysis did not see it as merely a technical mistake. According to those analyses, it was a broad failure of controls, procedures and management. The missile was on the pad, troubleshooting and launch preparations were going on together, and people who should have been in a safe place were gathered near the vehicle. On top of that, the 7 November deadline had weakened normal safety margins.

After the disaster the R-16 program paused but did not end. After the commission's report, work resumed in January 1961. The first successful flight took place on 2 February 1961, and on 1 November 1961 the missile reached initial operational capability. The R-16 served until 1976, and in 1965 it reached its peak of 202 deployed missiles. Mikhail Yangel's missile work did not stop either. The disaster slowed him, but the R-16 remained part of the race toward more powerful intercontinental missiles.

In the first half of the 1960s, a memorial to the 1960 dead was built at Baikonur. Even today, RKA officials visit it before a manned launch. On 20 December 1999, Russian president Boris Yeltsin posthumously awarded the Order of Courage to Nedelin and the other people involved in the disaster.

Exactly three years later, on 24 October 1963, another deadly accident struck Baikonur. This time an R-9 missile was being prepared in a silo at Site 70. The launch crew did not know that an oxygen leak had raised the partial oxygen pressure to 32%, when the maximum limit was 21%. A fire started by a spark from an electrical panel killed 7 people and destroyed the silo. For this reason 24 October came to be known as Baikonur's 'Black Day.' Since then, no launch has been attempted at Baikonur on 24 October, and the tradition continues today.

Many questions are still open. The biggest is the true number of dead, since sources give figures from 54 to 300. Perhaps the greatest lesson of this event is that safety rules, preparation and time pressure cannot coexist near a fuelled missile. With dangerous propellants like UDMH and RFNA, both highly corrosive and toxic, those rules matter even more. If you enjoyed this story, like the video and subscribe to the channel. shorts.roman: Aik fuelled rocket ke itne qareeb itne log kyun thay? 24 October 1960 ko Baikonur mein prototype R-16 pad 41 par khara tha. Pre-launch testing jari thi. Phir main sequencer mein kharabi aayi. Second stage ka engine pad par hi ignite ho gaya. Is se neeche wala first stage phat gaya, aur bara dhamaka hua. Sarkari commission ke mutabiq 78 log jaan se gaye, jin mein 74 mauqe par thay. Missile designer Mikhail Yangel bach gaye. Woh chand sau meter door bunker ke peechay cigarette peene gaye thay. Baad mein commission ne paya ke pad par zaroorat se bohat zyada log mojood thay. Magar is ke baad kya chhupaya gaya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 24 October 1960 a prototype R-16 fired its second-stage engine on the pad at Baikonur.
The accident is known as the Nedelin catastrophe.

shorts.titleEn: The Plane Crash That Never Happened
shorts.text: Marshal Nedelin کی موت کی خبر جھوٹی کیوں دی گئی؟ 24 October 1960 کے حادثے کے فوراً بعد Nikita Khrushchev نے مکمل secrecy نافذ کر دی۔ سرکاری news release میں کہا گیا کہ Nedelin ایک plane crash میں جان سے گئے۔ دوسرے engineers کے خاندانوں کو بھی یہی کہنے کا مشورہ دیا گیا۔ سوچیں، اپنے پیاروں کی اصل کہانی بھی کھل کر نہیں بتا سکتے تھے۔ Khrushchev نے Leonid Brezhnev کو investigation commission کا سربراہ بنا کر موقع پر بھیجا۔ Brezhnev نے کہا کہ ہم کسی کو trial پر نہیں لائیں گے۔ سوویت یونین نے یہ واقعہ 1989 تک تسلیم نہیں کیا۔ تو سچ آخر کیسے سامنے آیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Marshal Nedelin ki maut ki khabar jhooti kyun di gayi? 24 October 1960 ke hadse ke foran baad Nikita Khrushchev ne mukammal secrecy nafiz kar di. Sarkari news release mein kaha gaya ke Nedelin aik plane crash mein jaan se gaye. Dusray engineers ke khandanon ko bhi yahi kehne ka mashwara diya gaya. Sochein, apne pyaron ki asal kahani bhi khul kar nahin bata sakte thay. Khrushchev ne Leonid Brezhnev ko investigation commission ka sarbarah bana kar mauqe par bheja. Brezhnev ne kaha ke hum kisi ko trial par nahin layenge. Soviet Union ne yeh waqia 1989 tak tasleem nahin kiya. To sach aakhir kaise samne aaya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
After the 1960 Baikonur accident, Khrushchev ordered total secrecy and Nedelin's death was reported as a plane crash.
The Soviet Union did not acknowledge the event until 1989.

shorts.text: ایک ہی حادثہ، اور death toll کے کئی مختلف اعداد! کیوں؟ Nedelin catastrophe کے بارے میں ہر source الگ تعداد بتاتا ہے۔ December 1960 میں Italian agency Continentale نے 100 لوگوں کی خبر دی۔ 1965 میں The Guardian نے جاسوس Oleg Penkovsky کے حوالے سے 300 تک بتایا۔ 1989 کے بعد سوویت حکومت نے 54 کہا۔ Roscosmos نے 126 کا اندازہ دیا، مگر کہا کہ یہ 60 سے 150 کے درمیان بھی ہو سکتا ہے۔ جبکہ 1994 کی state commission رپورٹ میں 78 لوگ درج ہیں۔ یعنی کوئی ایک حتمی عدد موجود نہیں۔ دوستو، یہ فرق اتنا بڑا کیوں ہے؟ کیونکہ برسوں تک سچ ہی چھپایا گیا تھا۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Aik hi hadsa, aur death toll ke kai mukhtalif adaad! Kyun? Nedelin catastrophe ke bare mein har source alag tadad batata hai. December 1960 mein Italian agency Continentale ne 100 logon ki khabar di. 1965 mein The Guardian ne jasoos Oleg Penkovsky ke hawale se 300 tak bataya. 1989 ke baad Soviet hukumat ne 54 kaha. Roscosmos ne 126 ka andaza diya, magar kaha ke yeh 60 se 150 ke darmiyan bhi ho sakta hai. Jabke 1994 ki state commission report mein 78 log darj hain. Yani koi aik hatmi adad mojood nahin. Dosto, yeh farq itna bara kyun hai? Kyunke barson tak sach hi chhupaya gaya tha. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
